articles.title: Jamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils
articles.summary: Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal Of course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal

O f course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night.

320g frozen spinach 1 onion (160g) Olive oil 300g dried macaroni 50g plain flour 2 heaped tsp English mustard 500ml semi-skimmed milk Salt and black pepper 400g frozen fish pie mix , from sustainable sources 100g cheddar 2 red chicory 60g rocket Red-wine vinegar Extra-virgin olive oil

Turn on the grill to high. Boil the kettle. Defrost the spinach in a bowl in the microwave. Peel and finely chop the onion, and place in a large ovenproof frying pan on a high heat with one tablespoon of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, for five minutes, or until soft. Cook the pasta in a pan of boiling salted water for eight minutes, until al dente, then drain, reserving a mugful of the starchy cooking water.

Stir the flour and mustard into the onions, then gradually stir in the milk. Add the spinach to the pan, water and all, then season. Stir in the fish chunks and simmer for five minutes on a medium heat, then stir in the drained pasta, along with a splash of the reserved water, if needed. Coarsely grate and mix in half the cheese, grating the rest over the top. Carefully transfer to the highest shelf of the grill for a few minutes, until golden and bubbling.

Meanwhile, finely slice the chicory bases and separate the leaves, toss with the rocket and a tablespoon each of red-wine vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil, then season. Serve with the fish pie pasta bake.

4 garlic cloves 1 fresh red chilli Olive oil 500g ripe tomatoes 1 460g jar roast red peppers ½ pomegranate 30g shelled unsalted pistachios 1 bunch dill (20g) 4 flatbreads 2 400g tins lentils Red-wine vinegar Salt and black pepper 100g feta

Peel the garlic and finely slice with the chilli, then put in a shallow casserole pan on a medium-high heat with two tablespoons of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, until soft but not coloured. Chop and add the tomatoes. Tip the peppers, juice and all, into a blender, blitz smooth, then pour into the pan. Cook, stirring occasionally, for eight minutes, or until thickened.

Meanwhile, hold the pomegranate half cut side down in your palm and bash the back of it so the seeds tumble out into a bowl. Finely chop the pistachios. Pick and chop the dill. Warm the flatbreads.

Drain the lentils and add to the pan with a half-tablespoon of red-wine vinegar. Simmer for a final five minutes, then stir through half the pomegranate seeds and half the chopped dill, and season.

Scatter over the pistachios and the remaining pomegranate seeds, crumble over the feta, and sprinkle over the remaining dill. Serve with warm flatbreads.

These recipes are edited extracts from 20-Minute Meals by Jamie Oliver, published by Penguin Michael Joseph © Jamie Oliver Enterprises Limited (2026, 20MM) at £30. To order a copy for £25.50, visit guardianbookshop.com

articles.title: Granit Xhaka admits to receiving fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022
articles.summary: Sunderland captain withdrawn from Switzerland squad He will be questioned by prosecutor’s office in Lucerne Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022. The Sunderland and Switzerland captain – who was an Arsenal player at the time – has apologised for this “mistake” and will sit out his country’s forthcoming four Nations League matches. Xhaka is poised to be questioned by the prosecutor’s office in Lucerne next week as it decides whether any criminal proceedings will be initiated regarding the alleged issue of a series of false Covid certificates by a doctor based in the Swiss city during the pandemic. The doctor, who was first investigated in 2023, has denied the allegations. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022. The Sunderland and Switzerland captain – who was an Arsenal player at the time – has apologised for this “mistake” and will sit out his country’s forthcoming four Nations League matches.

Xhaka is poised to be questioned by the prosecutor’s office in Lucerne next week as it decides whether any criminal proceedings will be initiated regarding the alleged issue of a series of false Covid certificates by a doctor based in the Swiss city during the pandemic. The doctor, who was first investigated in 2023, has denied the allegations.

In a statement issued via Instagram, Xhaka acknowledged he had decided not to be inoculated against the virus. “In recent days there has been much reporting about a matter from my past. I would like to address this personally,” he wrote. “At the time, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns regarding the Covid-19 vaccination. I felt deep distrust of the vaccine and was plagued by fear and uncertainty.

“In this turbulent emotional state, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of clarifying my open questions through the proper channels. Today I clearly see this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry. I take responsibility for this decision, am committed to investigating the matter and am co-operating with the relevant authorities”. Xhaka tested positive for Covid in September 2022 and the 33-year-old – he turns 34 on Sunday – did not feature in Switzerland’s internationals that month.

A spokesperson for the Lucerne Cantonal Prosector’s Office said: “The aim [of the inquiries] is to clarify whether there has been conduct relevant under criminal law in connection with the possible fraudulent obtaining of a false certification and/or document forgery.”

Should charges be brought, Xhaka could face a heavy fine or, theoretically, a five-year prison sentence. However, the imposition of the latter sanction – or any sort of custodial punishment – is understood to be extremely unlikely.

Given that Xhaka was with Arsenal in 2022, Sunderland have told the Guardian they are not commenting on the matter. The midfielder left north London to join Bayer Leverkusen in 2023 and arrived at the Stadium of Light two years later.

Xhaka, who has been capped 152 times by Switzerland, will now miss the impending Nations League matches away to North Macedonia and Scotland and at home against Slovenia and North Macedonia.

articles.title: Cole Palmer injury likely to scupper his England return in Nations League
articles.summary: Rashford and Mainoo doubts for Spain opener Livramento also expected to withdraw from squad Cole Palmer will withdraw from the England squad with a minor muscle injury while there is a doubt over whether Marcus Rashford will be able to be involved. The Manchester United winger held the area by the front of his hip and groin as he walked off slowly after his substitution at Fulham on Sunday. Palmer was given a high-profile recall by Thomas Tuchel on Friday for the forthcoming Nations League fixtures, when the manager and his players will take their first steps on the new two-year cycle that they hope will end in glory at Euro 2028. England are back in Nations League Group A and kick off against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. They then play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Cole Palmer will withdraw from the England squad with a minor muscle injury while there is a doubt over whether Marcus Rashford will be able to be involved. The Manchester United winger held the area by the front of his hip and groin as he walked off slowly after his substitution at Fulham on Sunday.

Palmer was given a high-profile recall by Thomas Tuchel on Friday for the forthcoming Nations League fixtures, when the manager and his players will take their first steps on the new two-year cycle that they hope will end in glory at Euro 2028. England are back in Nations League Group A and kick off against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. They then play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Tuchel omitted Palmer from his World Cup squad after the Chelsea midfielder’s form ebbed last season. The manager preferred Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Eberechi Eze as the No 10s. He has retained the trio for this elongated international window and added Palmer after his fine form since the beginning of the season. The 24-year-old has contributed four goals and two assists for Chelsea and been a virtual ever-present for them. Yet he is once again expected to miss out with England . Palmer has made only three appearances under Tuchel; he has been frequently undermined by injury.

Tuchel has always championed Rashford; he called him up when he named his first squad in March of last year and the player was struggling for form. Tuchel wanted to show the 28-year-old that he believed in him and he has always included him when he has been available. Tuchel seemed to lose a bit of faith after Rashford played poorly against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup this summer. Thereafter, Tuchel barely used him until England’s semi-final exit against Argentina, giving him a couple of minutes as a stoppage-time substitute in that game but nothing more. He did play him for the first 45 minutes of the third place playoff against France.

Kobbie Mainoo, Rashford’s United teammate, is also a doubt for the upcoming England fixtures while the Newcastle full-back Tino Livramento is expected to withdraw. Livramento was forced to pull out of the World Cup squad with a calf injury and he only returned for his club as a substitute against Bournemouth at the start of the month. He suffered a set-back in training before Newcastle’s win over Hull on Saturday and was not in the match-day squad. Livramento is yet to start a game this season.

Mainoo was in the World Cup squad but he was the only outfield player not to get a single minute on the pitch. Tuchel said last Friday that it was entirely on him; it was no slight on Mainoo’s ability or levels of application. The manager said he would certainly give Mainoo minutes in at least one of the upcoming games.

articles.title: Harry Styles walked eight miles in loafers. Is he ruining his feet? There’s only one way to find out
articles.summary: For his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against it Last month, just before his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, Harry Styles was spotted walking the streets of New York. According to the paparazzi who trailed him throughout his journey, he walked eight miles – all the way from Brooklyn into Manhattan – in loafers. If, like me, you own a pair of loafers, your first thought is probably: that doesn’t sound like a good idea. On Instagram, Grazia called Styles’ shoes “perhaps the least sensible footwear for such an undertaking”. Continue reading...
articles.content:
For his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against it

L ast month, just before his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, Harry Styles was spotted walking the streets of New York. According to the paparazzi who trailed him throughout his journey, he walked eight miles – all the way from Brooklyn into Manhattan – in loafers.

If, like me, you own a pair of loafers, your first thought is probably: that doesn’t sound like a good idea. On Instagram, Grazia called Styles’ shoes “perhaps the least sensible footwear for such an undertaking”.

You might imagine that single outing would have taught Styles a lesson, but he was photographed a few days later in the same pair of loafers, which all the evidence suggests are dark brown, pre-distressed Prada “Shuffle” shoes that cost £910. At that price I wouldn’t even wear them outside – they look soft and flimsy, like a cross between a moccasin and a ballet slipper.

However, following Styles’ example, I’m suddenly determined to get more mileage out of my own, underused slip-ons. I mean to wear them every day, all day, for a week – and to walk at least eight miles in them, if not in one day, then at least cumulatively.

But first I have a question: could it be bad for my feet? What are the actual risks of such an undertaking?

“A loafer by construction has a smaller volume in the forefoot than a shoe that has a substantial fastening,” says Dr Helen Branthwaite, chief clinical advisor at the Royal College of Podiatry. In other words, a slip-on shoe is narrow at the front because, without laces or straps, it’s the only way it can hold on to your foot. “This may cause some compression to the toes if the shape and volume of the front of the shoe is not the same as the wearer’s foot.”

I send a link to a Styles/loafer pap shot to Christophe Champs, an orthotics specialist and the founder of the Podo clinic in London. “The main problem I see in that picture is a summer look,” he says. “Summer is the worst season for us.” Pounding hard city pavements in insubstantial shoes with no heel contour or arch support – slippers, loafers, flip-flops – can cause real problems. During this past hot summer, Champs says his clinic saw a fivefold increase in patients presenting with plantar fasciitis – a painful inflammation of the tissue connecting your heel to your toes.

For a couple of years the fashion world has remarked upon a gradual decline in the number of trainers appearing at runway shows, and the corresponding trend for loafers. “The younger customer is asking for styles that were particularly hot in the 1970s,” shoemaker Tim Little, owner of footwear brand Grenson, told Esquire in January. “Thin, slim-soled, often tasselled, and, above all easy on the feet.” GQ also recently declared that loafers were the “ most crucial shoes of 2026 ”.

It’s raining the first time I decide to wear my loafers all day, and I’m pretty footsore by suppertime, having covered no more than three miles. Along the way I’ve experienced both toe compression and heel slippage. But the shoes also hurt because I’ve never worn them long enough to break them in properly, even though I bought them years ago. Mine are sturdy, thick-soled penny loafers, quite unlike Styles’ pair.

Styles’ shoes, I’ve come to understand, are a fashionable slip-on subset sometimes known as a “scrunch loafer”. They’re so completely without structure that they look as if they’ve been run over by a steamroller. Perversely, Styles’ loafers have laces.

But, according to Champs, there is a bigger and more common problem than walking eight miles in scrunch loafers: the widespread habit of wearing running shoes on one’s daily commute. He says the soles of most cheap modern trainers are too high, too light and too cushioned to provide proper support. “You look at people from behind and it’s painful,” he says. “They’re on big fat sponges. So at least Harry doesn’t have this.”

His compromise recommendation for men’s walk-to-work footwear is a well-made dress shoe. “It’s time now to bring patients back into dress shoes,” he says. “But when my patients see my shoes they tell me, ‘Christophe, that for me is wedding and funeral.’” When he holds up his shoe to the Zoom camera for me, I’m surprised to see they’re not unlike my loafers, albeit with a pair of his own orthotic inserts tucked inside (Champs got into the orthotics game because of foot injuries he suffered as an athlete).

On my second day in loafers, I manage five miles in total, but by the evening I can feel my crowded fourth toes beginning to climb up over their larger neighbours. I’m beginning to see the appeal of Styles’ £910 slippers – at least your foot isn’t boxed in all day. And while it would probably be wise to alert fans to the dangers of emulating his choice of long-distance travelling shoe, it doesn’t mean it’s necessarily a problem for Styles himself.

“If Harry Styles is comfortable in loafers, and he can dance and walk in them, then he must have a strong foot, with a complementary shape to the shoe in question,” says Branthwaite, pointing out that Styles is a trained performer. “If someone else wishes to walk eight miles in his shoes, then they would also need to do the same training and practice.”

In Champs’ opinion, Styles’ footwear, while wholly inappropriate for an eight-mile hike, is by no means the worst option. “Those shoes are not so bad for a short walk,” he says. “It’s actually more dangerous to wear decent shoes that are out of shape because they’ve been used for too long. Shoes need three things: to be recent, decent and laced up.”

That’s enough advice to persuade me to give up my loafer marathon halfway through day three, and long before I’ve walked eight miles in them. Then again, looking at all the other shoes in my cupboard, it’s possible they’re still my best bet.

Later I was made aware of even more recent paparazzi shots that showed Styles wearing flat-soled light blue trainers. Maybe he’s learned his lesson after all.

Mine are sturdy, thick-soled penny loafers, quite unlike Styles’ pair.

Styles’ shoes, I’ve come to understand, are a fashionable slip-on subset sometimes known as a “scrunch loafer”. They’re so completely without structure that they look as if they’ve been run over by a steamroller. Perversely, Styles’ loafers have laces.

But, according to Champs, there is a bigger and more common problem than walking eight miles in scrunch loafers: the widespread habit of wearing running shoes on one’s daily commute. He says the soles of most cheap modern trainers are too high, too light and too cushioned to provide proper support. “You look at people from behind and it’s painful,” he says. “They’re on big fat sponges. So at least Harry doesn’t have this.”

His compromise recommendation for men’s walk-to-work footwear is a well-made dress shoe. “It’s time now to bring patients back into dress shoes,” he says. “But when my patients see my shoes they tell me, ‘Christophe, that for me is wedding and funeral.’” When he holds up his shoe to the Zoom camera for me, I’m surprised to see they’re not unlike my loafers, albeit with a pair of his own orthotic inserts tucked inside (Champs got into the orthotics game because of foot injuries he suffered as an athlete).

On my second day in loafers, I manage five miles in total, but by the evening I can feel my crowded fourth toes beginning to climb up over their larger neighbours. I’m beginning to see the appeal of Styles’ £910 slippers – at least your foot isn’t boxed in all day. And while it would probably be wise to alert fans to the dangers of emulating his choice of long-distance travelling shoe, it doesn’t mean it’s necessarily a problem for Styles himself.

“If Harry Styles is comfortable in loafers, and he can dance and walk in them, then he must have a strong foot, with a complementary shape to the shoe in question,” says Branthwaite, pointing out that Styles is a trained performer. “If someone else wishes to walk eight miles in his shoes, then they would also need to do the same training and practice.”

In Champs’ opinion, Styles’ footwear, while wholly inappropriate for an eight-mile hike, is by no means the worst option. “Those shoes are not so bad for a short walk,” he says. “It’s actually more dangerous to wear decent shoes that are out of shape because they’ve been used for too long. Shoes need three things: to be recent, decent and laced up.”

That’s enough advice to persuade me to give up my loafer marathon halfway through day three, and long before I’ve walked eight miles in them. Then again, looking at all the other shoes in my cupboard, it’s possible they’re still my best bet.
Later I was made aware of even more recent paparazzi shots that showed Styles wearing flat-soled light blue trainers. Maybe he’s learned his lesson after all.

articles.title: WSL talking points: Arsenal’s attacking woes and Goodwin makes England case
articles.summary: Gunners are held to second home draw in two weeks, while Spurs smash Palace 7-0 to maintain strong start After being unable to find a way through Crystal Palace’s backline last time out, Arsenal were again frustrated at home in a draw with Manchester United on Saturday and Renée Slegers was asked post-match about how her team can turn their dominance of possession and territory into more goals. It could have been worse, of course, if Smilla Holmberg had not made it 1-1 in the 95th minute. “It’s not one thing, it’s a combination of things,” Slegers said. “It’s a cocktail of things, there are some details in decision making, some details in the technical execution. It’s also the ruthlessness in front of goal but I know the players want it and they want to do that, they want to execute for Arsenal.” Tom Garry Match report: Arsenal 1-1 Manchester United Match report: Manchester City 4-2 Liverpool Continue reading...
articles.content:
Gunners are held to second home draw in two weeks, while Spurs smash Palace 7-0 to maintain strong start

After being unable to find a way through Crystal Palace’s backline last time out, Arsenal were again frustrated at home in a draw with Manchester United on Saturday and Renée Slegers was asked post-match about how her team can turn their dominance of possession and territory into more goals. It could have been worse, of course, if Smilla Holmberg had not made it 1-1 in the 95th minute. “It’s not one thing, it’s a combination of things,” Slegers said. “It’s a cocktail of things, there are some details in decision making, some details in the technical execution. It’s also the ruthlessness in front of goal but I know the players want it and they want to do that, they want to execute for Arsenal.” Tom Garry

Just over a week before Sarina Wiegman names her Lionesses squad for October’s World Cup play-off tie against Greece, the England Under-23 international Isobel Goodwin did her chances of a first senior selection no harm at all, as she scored twice for London City Lionesses in a comprehensive 4-1 victory at Charlton. The 23-year-old, who linked up well with Alexia Putellas, scored five times in the WSL last term but will be keen to exceed that this season and impress Wiegman, particularly at a time when Chelsea’s Aggie Beever-Jones has been out with a minor ankle injury and Arsenal’s Michelle Agyemang is still returning from her ACL. Wiegman may be considering alternative options for a backup striker to Alessia Russo for these key fixtures. TG

She was the WSL’s leading assist-provider in the 2023-24 and 2024-25 seasons and supplied the joint-second highest number of assists last season, but goals were not coming regularly for the England winger Lauren Hemp, who had not scored in the WSL since last November until she decisively found the net twice on Friday night in a 4-2 win over Liverpool. The Manchester City boss, Andrée Jeglertz, heaped praise on Hemp as he told Sky Sports: “She’s an amazing player. I don’t know what she’s made of, because she just loves to be on the field and looks like she has so much energy. She’s a game-changer.” Hemp nearly had a hat-trick but she saw an early, rising strike tipped over the bar by Khiara Keating. TG

There has been plenty of debate in recent months about the future of young English players in theWSL and whether they are being hampered by limited opportunities. England’s Lexi Potter, however, is one such young talent who has been catching the eye at the heart of Chelsea’s midfield. The 2-0 win over Birmingham City was her second start in as many matches and she produced yet another assured performance. The 20-year-old’s calmness and ability to work in tight spaces enables her to escape pressure while the timing of her runs into the box is a huge asset. She opened the scoring at Stamford Bridge by being alert to the second ball in the area while her burgeoning relationship with Keira Walsh has been notable. “They understand each other, and even when they are on the pitch and they close their eyes, they know where each other is,” Sonia Bompastor told Chelsea media. Like Goodwin, may she have done enough to catch Wiegman’s eye? Sophie Downey

Olivia Holdt marked her first start of the season by scoring a hat-trick as Spurs turned a dominant but goalless first half into a 7-0 win at Crystal Palace. Palace’s task was made harder when Fuka Tsunoda was sent off in the seventh minute following a reckless challenge on Cathinka Tandberg, but Spurs initially struggled to break down a side defending deep. “When they got the red card, I was thinking this could actually be tougher for us,” Holdt said. At half-time, the Spurs manager, Martin Ho, asked his players to get more bodies into the box. Holdt had completed her hat-trick by the 73rd minute as Spurs finally found the ruthlessness that had been missing. Mitul Samji

Brighton may have had 25 shots, eight on target and an xG of 3.17, but they were forced to settle for a 1-1 draw against Aston Villa after failing to make their dominance count. Gabby George’s first goal for the club gave them a deserved lead in the 31st minute, but they could not find a second despite creating a total of 15 chances. The result was made all the more frustrating by the manner of Villa’s equaliser in the 89th minute, with Brighton unable to defend a corner. The result leaves the new manager, Arturo Ruiz, still searching for their first win of the season. “Here in our stadium, in these kinds of games we cannot lose two points,” he said. “We need to get three points in 100% of these games.” The performance was encouraging, but the finishing was not. Réshma Rao

articles.title: Tories pledge to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists
articles.summary: The party says scrapping the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations.
articles.content:
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul visited Bicester Village, a designer outlet shopping centre popular with tourists, to promote the policy

The Conservative Party has pledged to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists from outside the European Union.

The Tories said the decision to scrap the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations.

Leader Kemi Badenoch, who was a Treasury minister when the tax relief was abolished, said businesses were being "let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away".

The VAT Retail Export Scheme - which allowed overseas visitors to get a VAT refund on items they had bought in Great Britain and took home in their luggage - was scrapped for non-EU visitors under the previous Conservative government in 2021, while it was also not extended for EU visitors.

At the time, Badenoch said it was "a costly relief which does not benefit the whole of GB equally".

However, the Conservatives have now set out plans to restore VAT refunds for eligible visitors from outside the EU.

The party said that if evidence confirms the scheme "pays its way", this would be extended to visitors from the EU by the end of the next Parliament.

It said the cost of reintroducing the scheme would be offset by cracking down on "NHS health tourism", including more consistent charging of patients ineligible for free treatment, minimum recovery targets for debts and requiring full repayment of debts before visa applications or renewals will be considered.

The remaining costs would be funded from a package of savings set out by the Tories last year.

The party also argued the move would benefit shops, hotels, restaurants and the wider tourism industry.

It pointed to research by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (Cebr), which suggested fully restoring tax-free shopping for tourists could attract up to 2.35 million extra visitors and generate £4.1bn in extra spending.

The report from earlier this month also estimated that for every £1 of VAT refunded, this could generate £1.54 in other taxes.

Badenoch said: "We have iconic retailers, inventive designers and brilliant manufacturers, but they are being let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away.

"Holidaymakers are choosing rival cities in other countries for the simple reason that it saves them money."

Businesses have long called for tax-free shopping for tourists to be reintroduced, arguing they are at a disadvantage to other European countries.

EU countries offer VAT refunds for non-EU visitors, while other European countries such as Switzerland have similar schemes.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive at the British Retail Consortium, said: "Introducing a modern tax-free shopping scheme would help attract more international spending to the UK, supporting high streets, jobs and investment in towns and cities across the country.

"Done properly, it would boost economic growth and deliver a net benefit to the Exchequer."

However, a Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch used to say tax-free shopping was a costly giveaway and now she's trying to sell it as an economic miracle.

"If they really think it's such a great idea, they should explain why they scrapped it in the first place and how they'd pay for bringing it back."

articles.title: Shaun Edwards finally lands England coaching role after joining Red Roses
articles.summary: Defence guru left French men’s team in June Edwards will work as a consultant for duration of WXV Defence guru Shaun Edwards has joined the Red Roses coaching set-up in a consultancy role until the end of the WXV Global Series. The former Wales and France men’s coach has not had a role in women’s rugby before but has been brought on board with the Red Roses head coach, John Mitchell, describing his credentials as “exceptional” in the highest echelons of the sport. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Defence guru Shaun Edwards has joined the Red Roses coaching set-up in a consultancy role until the end of the WXV Global Series.

The former Wales and France men’s coach has not had a role in women’s rugby before but has been brought on board with the Red Roses head coach, John Mitchell, describing his credentials as “exceptional” in the highest echelons of the sport.

The 59-year-old Edwards is already in situ and will help the team as they prepare to take on New Zealand at Allianz Stadium this Saturday before travelling with the squad to the Canada and the USA next month.

Edwards, who played rugby league for Wigan Warriors and Great Britain, left his role with France in June after more than six years when Fabien Galthié restructured Les Bleus’ backroom staff.

Mitchell said: “Since his time with France ended, we have had a conversation about our game, and he expressed an interest in working in an international women’s setup for the first time. He has a huge amount of respect for the Red Roses and what we stand for; he sees it as a privilege to join our environment.

“His coaching credentials are exceptional and his experience at the highest level of the game speaks for itself. Defensively, Sarah Hunter [England’s defence coach] is relishing the opportunity to learn from him, alongside the rest of our coaching group, as we head into another exciting Test match against New Zealand. Shaun will add to the programme and provide incredible value to the girls over the remainder of the WXV Global Series.”

Edwards began his coaching career in rugby union at the Premiership club Wasps, first joining as a defence and backs coach in 2001. He was promoted to head coach in 2005 and the club won the Heineken Cup and Premiership during his tenure.

He then moved to Wales as a defence coach in 2011 and won four Six Nations titles, three of which were Grand Slams, alongside the head coach Warren Gatland.

Edwards signed on as the French defence coach in 2020 and won three Six Nations titles with the team. The coach cannot win a trophy with the Red Roses as the WXV is a series of matches with no silverware. However, he can help to get their victory record back on track after their 39-game winning streak came to an end last Saturday after drawing 26-26 against Canada .

England will play the Black Ferns – who were the last team to beat the Red Roses in the World Cup final in 2022 – in front of more than 50,000 this weekend.

articles.content:
When my husband and I adopted her, Bud had to go on a strict diet. Thankfully, she got healthy and became the diva everyone loves today

B ud came into my life at the start of the Covid pandemic in 2020. I work at RSPCA Norwich as head of animal welfare and, when we all had to work from home, I offered to foster Bud, a blue-fronted amazon parrot . My husband and I thought it would be a short-term thing, but by the time the pandemic had settled down we had really bonded with her, so she never left.

Back then, Bud had a crisp addiction and was too overweight to fly. She was about 200g heavier than a parrot should be. We had to put her on a strict diet because she had some health concerns – we found a lipoma, a fatty lump, on her keel bone (which runs down from the breast); it doesn’t bother her, but we still have to monitor it. Thankfully, she has lost weight; her feathers are all better quality and she loves her life.

Some parrots like constant human interaction, but Bud enjoys her own space. She has just turned 28 (parrots can live for 50 to 60 years) and is a bit of a diva. Bud knows what she wants and when she wants it. She can be the most endearing creature in the world, and then suddenly have a tantrum like a toddler. She can be quite challenging, but she is really lovely.

She has a great sense of comedic timing. When I’m speaking to my neighbours, she will sometimes shout “Bye!” in the middle of a conversation and they think someone is asking them to leave. articles.summary: Brand returns to its physical and unconventional roots as it battles undergoes stark restructuring Back when a young Lee McQueen was showing at London fashion week, there was Dante, the show in a Hawksmoor church with a skeleton in the front row and a blaring soundtrack of organ music and gunfire. articles.content:
Brand returns to its physical and unconventional roots as it battles undergoes stark restructuring

B ack when a young Lee McQueen was showing at London fashion week , there was Dante, the show in a Hawksmoor church with a skeleton in the front row and a blaring soundtrack of organ music and gunfire. And there was Voss, where models were trapped inside a giant mirrored box set up as a psychiatric ward.

Twenty-five years later, the Alexander McQueen brand returned from the Paris schedule to a creepily beautiful subterranean 17th century London chapel, with steel harnesses, bulky ankle strapped heels that looked like electronic monitoring tags, and a chain mail dress of tiny silver skulls.

Darkness is a McQueen happy place. Which is fortunate, because dark times have come for the legendary brand. In the 2000s Lee McQueen was the toast of Paris, growing in sophistication and ambition, until tragedy struck in 2010.

After his death, the talent and emotional intelligence of his successor, Sarah Burton, who designed Kate Middleton’s wedding dress in 2011, kept the name riding high when many thought it would fall apart. But the McQueen name is now losing its heat and the brand is in trouble, undergoing a stark restructuring plan of shuttered stores and job losses.

Bringing McQueen home to the city where the name is still revered was the first decision made by Gianfranco d’Attis, who became the new chief executive in June, and the energy of this show proved it was the right call. McQueen hits different in London.

The new business strategy is to streamline and refocus McQueen: fewer trainers and sweatshirts, more evening gowns (red carpet remains a strength) and British tailoring. For the homecoming, the creative director, Seán McGirr, now in his third year at the brand, went deep into British references. He picked the vaulted undercroft venue because it felt like being inside his favourite painting in the National Gallery, Piero della Francesca’s The Baptism of Christ . Jackets paid homage to the radical tailoring of Tommy Nutter, Keith Flint hair horns to rave culture. “London is a constant stimulation,” he said backstage. “Style on the street is not conventional. I love the wrongness of it.”

McGirr is 38, with a dimpled smile and a soft Dublin accent. His instincts track lighter and sweeter than this house ever did in its reckless youth. Organza was whipped into meringue-like peaks at the shoulders of a corsetted ivory lace dress – he said he wanted the famous McQueen exaggerated shoulders “to look like angel wings. I wanted the message to feel ethereal, and light in a sense.”

The Roksanda show, at a rooftop garden next to the National Theatre, was a sunny contrast to McQueen, swathes of cherry- and lavender-coloured silk glinting under a blue sky. Thickly plaited rope belts in contrast colours were a tribute to the monumental fabric sculptures of Françoise Grossen, and a celebration of “the feminine energy of braiding, which is connected to hair, to craft, to housework”, the designer Roksanda Ilinčić said.

articles.title: The Joy of Six: epic sporting grudge matches
articles.summary: From F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting culture A boxing rivalry so intense that their sons got to copycat it 35 years later, yet the original is simply the best. That the preening, poetry-spouting, monocle-sporting, Jodhpur-wearing Eubank would irritate the rough-and-ready ex-squaddie Benn was hardly surprising. But the depth of the animosity was remarkable. articles.content:
From F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting culture

A boxing rivalry so intense that their sons got to copycat it 35 years later, yet the original is simply the best. That the preening, poetry-spouting, monocle-sporting, Jodhpur-wearing Eubank would irritate the rough-and-ready ex-squaddie Benn was hardly surprising. But the depth of the animosity was remarkable.

“I personally do hate him,” intoned Benn, exuding malevolence at the contract signing for their 1990 middleweight fight, shown live on ITV . Eubank, who refused to even look at his foe, demanded “some parliamentary procedure” – but there would be none shown in the ring on fight night. Benn’s ferocity forced the unbeaten but untested underdog to fight fire with fire. Eubank, swallowing blood from a badly cut tongue, rose from a knockdown in the eighth round to stop Benn in the ninth and take his WBO title.

In truth, the two Britons, who came from tough upbringings, had more in common than they cared to admit. But Eubank’s disdain for his profession – “a mug’s game” – antagonised Benn. Their 1993 rematch, which drew 43,000 people to Old Trafford and 16.5 million viewers on UK television, ended in a draw. It was their final in-ring fight but the two have made up, then fallen out again, several times since. We wouldn’t have it any other way.

Drive to Survive would give its right axle for a modern-day Formula One feud this bitter. The motor-mouthed, hot-tempered Piquet once referred to his fellow Brazilian Ayrton Senna as “a São Paulo taxi driver”. Yet Piquet’s dislike of his 1986-87 teammate Mansell raised his insults to the Shakespearean. “An uneducated blockhead,” was his view of his Williams partner, before Piquet tumbled into the gutter when referring to the British driver’s “stupid and ugly wife”.

Mansell understandably bristled at such appalling language and the pair focused so much on their own battles throughout the 1986 season that Alain Prost snuck in to claim the drivers’ championship. In 1987, the moustachioed Mansell won six races to Piquet’s three, yet the latter was rarely off the podium and lifted his third world title. It was their final season as teammates but bridges have been built in retirement. After several TV appearances together, Piquet conceded that in terms of titles: “I should have won in 86, he should have won in 87.”

Sir Alex Ferguson v Arsène Wenger, Brian Clough v Don Revie, Diego Simeone v anyone – manager rivalries are a rich tapestry. But few burned with such intensity as Guardiola v Mourinho, particularly during their two years in La Liga. Real Madrid brought in Mourinho in 2010; the ultimate win-at-all-costs pragmatist to dismantle Barcelona’s tiki-taka idealists. Familiarity quickly resulted in contempt between the pair, who had spent four years together at Barça when Guardiola was a player and Mourinho an interpreter and assistant coach.

“I hope one day he has the chance of winning a brilliant, clean championship with no scandal,” sneered Mourinho in 2011, as he accused Uefa of favouring Guardiola after a Champions League triumph. Cuttingly, he would later claim Guardiola’s baldness was a sign he “doesn’t enjoy football”. Barcelona won most of the head-to-head battles – including a 5-0 league thrashing – but the sniping exasperated Guardiola who called Mourinho “the fucking boss” of the press room, adding: “I try to learn from José on the pitch, but I prefer to learn as little as possible from him off the pitch.” In 2012, Madrid won La Liga with 100 points and a burned-out Guardiola stepped away from management for a year.

Yet the toll was just as great for Mourinho, who left Madrid in 2013. The anticipated rematch in Manchester failed to spark, despite Mourinho’s gripes at City’s “financial sharks” and unfair league titles. Their feud has mellowed in the years since, but it is doubtful the two will be chuckling away on their own Iberian football podcast (‘Pep Talk’?) in retirement.

“I think Serena hated me for being the skinny kid who beat her,” Sharapova wrote in her autobiography, recalling her breakthrough 2004 Wimbledon final win at age 17 . Well, Williams definitely hated that experience enough to win the next 19 matches against Sharapova, ending their rivalry with a staggering 20-2 win-loss record.

The American’s relentless dominance, raising her game to new heights against one foe in particular, seemed fuelled by something beyond on-court competition. That they reportedly dated the same player, Grigor Dimitrov, added personal heat. “Hey, if she wants to be with the guy with a black heart, go for it,” said Williams in 2013, while labelling Sharapova “so boring”.

Maria returned serve : “If she wants to talk about something personal, maybe she should talk about her relationship and her boyfriend that was married and is getting a divorce.” But Williams v Sharapova was bigger than any soap opera love triangle. It was a battle between the world’s best player and its most marketable; as if Williams – irked by the media attention paid to her 6ft, blond Russian adversary – had to remind everyone who the real era-defining athlete was. Happily, the two have actually become friends in retirement, with Sharapova asking Williams to induct her into the tennis hall of fame in 2025.

Cricket’s ultimate ‘Ian-off’ first began with a bar brawl in Melbourne in 1977, when England’s 21-year-old rising star Botham got into it with Australia’s former Test captain Chappell. The details have been vehemently disputed ever since. Beefy’s version is him punching Chappell to end his vile pommie-bashing. Chappell’s take is a hysterical young Botham lost the plot and pushed him off his chair, then threatened him with a glass.

They later clashed on the pitch – sledging, bouncers and send-offs – but it is away from the sporting arena that the rage has spilled over. More than 30 years of trading insults came to a head during the 2010-11 Ashes in Australia. Unable to walk past one another in a car park without some sly verbals, the two grandpas – combined age of 127 – went for each other and had to be restrained by their media colleagues. Three years ago a TV documentary, The Longest Feud: Chappell v Botham, brought no resolution with Chappell calling Botham “a coward”, while Sir Loin labelled his adversary “sad and lonely”. Sensational longevity.

Who didn’t the mercurial genius Higgins view as a loathed nemesis? Steve Davis (“I hate him”), Dennis Taylor (“I’ll have you shot”), Stephen Hendry (“Up your arse, you [c-word]”). Yet the greatest vitriol was saved for his polar opposite: snooker’s Canadian grinder, Thorburn. They played for money on Thorburn’s first day in England, which ended, Cliff recalled, with the Northern Irishman “at the top of the stairs with a ball in his hand about to throw it at me”.

Higgins won most of their matches but lost the biggest: the 1980 world championship final, when ‘the Hurricane’ blew a 9-5 lead to lose 18-16. Away from the table, during the 1983 Irish Open, Thorburn lamped Higgins and kicked him in the groin after being told he was “a Canadian [c-bomb] who is shit at snooker”. Five years later, the (ahem) famously clean-living Higgins accused Thorburn of utilising “bags of white powder”, ruining Cliff’s reputation.

For all the fallouts, a trace of respect endured. In 2009, a year before Higgins’ death, Thorburn won an embarrassingly one-sided legends match and was so upset at seeing his rival diminished that he shed a tear as they embraced afterwards.

articles.content:
Our photographer, Tom Jenkins, captures the colour and razzmatazz as college football arrived in the capital, hot on the heels of successful NFL outings in recent years

R arely has Wembley Way seen or heard such a commotion. The famous 500-yard long concourse leading to the national (association) football stadium in London played host to a sea of raucous American football fans on Saturday, as they gathered to mark the first ever top-tier college football game on British turf.

Pundits from Fox’s Big Noon Kickoff Show were broadcasting live from outside the venue – a curious spectacle in which the hosts even ate fish and chips on a temporary set that included a fake Grenadier guard and an old red phone box – as thousands of supporters around them waved placards and chanted college anthems. It fuelled a tailgate party atmosphere that wouldn’t have felt out of place in the States.

Dubbed the Union Jack Classic , the game pitted two sports-mad colleges, Kansas and Arizona State, against each other in front of 46,000 fans, with many of the players one day hoping to play in the NFL.

Crucially, Kenny Dillingham, the Arizona State coach, was also keen, says Hensey. “He’s a real character, a real visionary, and he said ‘I’ll play anyone, anywhere, anytime!’”

Above: Kansas marching band playing in the stands. Below: An Arizona fan makes the “forks up” sign that’s synonymous with the college.

Above: Kansas cheerleaders perform spectacular routines at pitchside. Below: Noah Ginsberg aka ‘Plunger Boy’, a well-known Kansas fan, in attendance at Wembley.

Below: Paige Blake, who played the national anthem on her electric guitar, waiting in the wings for her turn to perform.

The blueprint for the event was “to take some of the best traditional game day dynamics – the marching bands, the cheerleaders – and then add a bit of rock and roll, a little country, a little hip hop, and turn it into a concert with an American football game stuck in the middle of it,” says Hensey.

The razzmatazz began when the players emerged on to the field amid a tunnel of fireworks, before Paige Blake played the US national anthem on an electric guitar.

Every break in play was plugged with sound and colour as “spirit squads” including cheerleaders performed slick routines, while marching bands and musicians brought even more energy to proceedings – the latter leaving a footprint that will give the Wembley groundstaff a headache before England’s football match (or should that be soccer match) with Spain next weekend.

The fans – including 15,000 who travellled over from the States – created a partisan dynamic. Arizona supporters made their ‘Forks Up’ hand gesture to mimic the pitchfork on their emblem, while Kansas supporters bellowed their century-old battle-cry, Rock Chalk, which alludes to the chalky limestone that’s found on Mount Oread, where their campus is located.

The game itself was less eventful than the pageantry that surrounded it. Spanning more than three hours and 30 minutes, Arizona State won comfortably, despite the eventual 24-17 scoreline, with Jaren Hamilton running in a 100-yard kick-off return as the game swung decisively in their favour near the midway point.

Above: A Kansas attacking play during the Union Jack Classic. Below: Tackles, blocks and players looking hungry to impress the scouts.

Above: The Wembley arch is lit up in the colours of the two teams. Below: Kansas wide receiver Keaton Kubecka wearing the message “Kill or be killed” on a plaster over his nose.

Above: Arizona quarterback Cutter Boley tries to pass but is blocked by a leaping Leroy Harris III of Kansas. Below: The back of a helmet being worn by Kansas punter Ben Shipley, showing the words of the famous Kansas chant Rock Chalk; dejected Kansas players walk off after the final whistle.

College football players are used to big stadia. All of the teams in the Big 12 conference, to which Kansas and Arizona State belong, average crowds of more than 30,000 per home game, and some, like Brigham Young University, can attract north of 60,000.

But travelling to the UK and playing on the hallowed turf at Wembley was a unique thrill for the young players involved, the majority of whom didn’t even own passports prior to the trip.

“This was my first time going out of the United States,” said Kansas cornerback Jalen Todd. “Being from Detroit, I never expected to be playing football in the UK. Wembley is iconic.”

In the days before the game, both teams took a boat trip along the Thames and scaled Tower Bridge – the landmark that features on the Union Jack Classic winner’s trophy – to give them inspiration.

Above: Arizona State players pose over the glass window above Tower Bridge after taking a trip along the Thames from Putney Pier. Below: Players perform their famous “Forks Up” hand gesture and take selfies in front of the Houses of Parliament.

Below: Collecting burgers and fries before embarking on the boat trip; Arizona players on the Thames boat, backed the Houses of Parliament.

The Big 12 commissioner, Brett Yormark, says the event “exceeded” his expectations even though the crowd was well short of the anticipated 60,000, while Hensey says he is targeting a full stadium when they return with two new teams next year. “I personally think college football is on the cusp of what the NFL was 20, 30 years ago, and it’s about to go global,” he said.

For Dillingham, the greatest positive was the cultural impact of the trip on his players. “We had multiple players say ‘I love this place, London is awesome, I want to come back and spend summer or Christmas out here.’ It’s an experience that I think everybody will remember for the rest of their lives.”

Above: Daquwan Dunn, the defensive back for Arizona State, celebrates with a dance in front of teammates after the game. Below: Winning ASU head coach Kenny Dillingham talks to the media with his three-year-old son Kent on his shoulders.

Above: The trophy is removed from a protective box ready for the presentation. Below: Players from Arizona State and their mascot Sparky celebrate on the pitch with the trophy, which is shaped like Tower Bridge.

articles.content:
The Chargers star is huge, can run and has a golden right arm. But he has never quite reached the heights many expected for him

J ustin Herbert is one of the most promising quarterbacks in the NFL . In fact, Justin Herbert has forever been one of the most promising quarterbacks in the NFL. That adjective, “promising,” continued to be load-bearing on Sunday, as Herbert and his Chargers turned in an underwhelming performance in a 26-14 loss to the Raiders. Los Angeles are now 0-2 on the year, with those losses coming to the team that just picked No 1 in the draft and a moribund Arizona who picked No 3. Stockholders in Herbert’s growth were taking a beating in after-hours trading. But, as ever, there’s plenty of reason to debate whether Herbert underachieved or whether his team let him down.

Herbert is 6ft 6in, can run, has a golden right arm and is capable of making astonishing throws . NFL decision-makers view him as roughly the sixth-best QB in the league but also say things like , “He should have more accolades at this point.” Certainly, he should have more wins this season, but on Sunday the 28-year-old found himself outdueled by one of the league’s senior citizens in Vegas quarterback Kirk Cousins, who is 10 years his senior. Herbert completed 15 of 27 passes for a touchdown and two interceptions, and he also took three sacks. Cousins threw a pick and took two sacks but was much more efficient from down to down (8.7 yards per attempt to Herbert’s 7.1), and the Chargers offense mostly sputtered. In 13 possessions, Los Angeles put together two long touchdown drives and otherwise didn’t march more than 30 yards in a series.

How much of this is Herbert’s fault, though? It’s an eternal question, and one that came up after the Chargers’ playoff wildcard loss to the Patriots last season. In that game, Herbert played miserably but arguably had no chance not to be terrible, because the New England defenders were in his face all evening. In almost any Herbert loss, one can easily find examples of his teammates letting him down. Sunday was another good example. Herbert wasn’t terrific by any means, and given his billing, he’d ideally be able to get over failures by his teammates. But there’s not much the QB can do when tight end David Njoku bobbles a catch on an ever so slightly underthrown ball and turns it into an interception . Or when an under-pressure Herbert throws a ball that either of two receivers could catch without a problem, but one cuts off the other and drops it. Then there’s the injury luck – not so much to Herbert, who has generally been durable while playing through a number of injuries – but to those around him. Every year, a key member of his line or receiving corps seems to go down with a season-ending injury, leaving him exposed or without a weapon to deploy against opposing defenses. There are also question marks over the coaches who have overseen his career. Jim Harbaugh came to the Chargers with high expectations, but has yet to win a playoff game with the team, while Mike McDaniel, the team’s new offensive coordinator, has a reputation as a schematic whiz, but the Chargers offense has sputtered.

Herbert, of course, must shoulder some of the blame himself. The Chargers have not done a good job of protecting him, but the very best quarterbacks find a way to win even when the pocket collapses. He is also 0-3 in the playoffs – a small sample size, but it still raises question marks about how he performs against the very best teams. Unfortunately, this season there have been question marks against very average teams too.

The blame game will be in vogue this week. A team that we expected to contend with the Chiefs and Broncos for the AFC West have already dug themselves a substantial hole, and they’ve done it while using up one of the easiest stretches of schedule that any team will face all year. The Chargers are the only 0-2 team in the division and one of just four in the AFC. To recover, they’ll need Herbert to be Superman. He has that gear, but consistency remains elusive, and the team’s margin for error is now awfully thin.

Brock Purdy, QB, San Francisco 49ers. According to ESPN’s QBR ratings, Purdy had one of the 10 best games by a quarterback since the rankings began in 2006 (in case you’re wondering, the best was from Carson Palmer in 2009 ). Admittedly, Purdy was playing against the Dolphins on Sunday but he was superb: he completed 20 of his 22 passes for 287 yards and two touchdowns. He was also his team’s leading rusher with 30 yards and a touchdown on three carries. This came after another three-touchdown performance in the season opener against the No Sleep Till Melbourne Los Angeles Rams. Most of us expected the Niners to settle for a wildcard place out of the stacked NFC West this season but at this rate they could take the division.

56. How many fewer points the Bears scored in their loss to the Vikings on Sunday, as compared to in their 59-37 romp over Carolina in Week 1. Chicago entered the week on as much of a spiritual high as the franchise has enjoyed in decades but ended it in a much more concerning place. Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores had Caleb Williams and the offense in a blender all afternoon, and then things got considerably worse in the fourth quarter. That’s when Williams injured his hamstring, seriously enough that he wasn’t putting weight on his right leg as he walked off the field. (Reporters did see him walking under his own power as he left the locker room later.) Bears head coach Ben Johnson said he was “happy it’s nothing with the knee,” ruling out a torn ACL, and that the team would learn more on Monday.

The Steelers’ dreadful offense painted their masterpiece on a third-and-7 at the Patriots’ 22-yard line, in a game that CBS subject millions to as its national game of the week with Jim Nantz and JJ Watt in the booth. Trailing 10-0 in the second quarter, Aaron Rodgers took a shotgun snap and quickly found himself in a New England situation, as his blockers let pass rushers converge from both his left and right. What followed was a circus. Both teams booted the ball on the ground for a solid seven seconds. The catastrophe came to a humorous end when the Steelers’ left tackle, 317-pounder Troy Fautanu, fell on the ball for a loss of 36 yards that pushed Pittsburgh out of field-goal range. The Patriots went on to a 20-3 win. The Steelers’ offense looks even worse this year under 42-year-old Rodgers and his once-and-present head coach, the supposed offensive thinker Mike McCarthy.

Williams wasn’t the only top-two pick from the 2024 draft to get hurt. Commanders QB Jayden Daniels did not make it through his team’s 37-20 loss at the Cowboys. Particularly upsetting was the location of his injury: the same left elbow that Daniels dislocated last season. An offensive lineman stepped on Daniels’s foot during an under-center exchange, and he appeared to hurt the elbow while trying to break his fall to the turf. A replay of Daniels’s elbow bending in the wrong direction prompted a relatable exclamation of “oh shit” from Tom Brady, watching from the Fox booth. Daniels throws with his right arm (ie: not the one injured here), but that’s only of mild comfort to the Commanders. Washington head coach Dan Quinn said after the game that Daniels had indeed dislocated his elbow again, although no bones were broken. The quarterback is expected to return at some point this season.

Spare a thought for the players in the Eagles’ win over the Titans in Nashville. Fox reported that the turf (not the air) temperature reached 157F (69.4C) and some players’ cleats even melted . “It was hot as shit, everybody was as hot as shit,” Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said after his team’s 24-20 win. “I didn’t play a snap and I had to get an IV.”

The Browns beat the Buccaneers behind an unusually competent effort from their pitiful quarterback, Deshaun Watson. The QB on the losing end was Baker Mayfield, whom the Browns chased off after 2021 so that they could sign Watson to the worst contract in football history. Watson has spent his Browns career either injured, ineffective, or suspended after the league looked into allegations of serial sexual misconduct. Watson’s 24-of-30 effort for 238 yards and two touchdowns doesn’t absolve him, or the Browns, of anything but does save the franchise a bit of short-term embarrassment that would have come with Mayfield beating them.

The Panthers enjoyed one of the most dominant wins of the young season, a 34-3 destruction of a Falcons team that again started third-string QB Cooper Rush (and also played training camp darling Jack Strand, an undrafted rookie from Division II Minnesota State-Moorhead). The story here was about a QB with a more robust pedigree: Bryce Young, whose career looks like it might amount to something after all. The 2023 No 1 pick came on strong in the last few months of last season and played well. Young averaged eight yards per throw while avoiding interceptions. Even better, Young’s sharpest connection was with 2025 first-round wideout Tetairoa McMillan, who torched Atlanta corner AJ Terrell for a 26-yard completion in the first three minutes and went on to a 101-yard day. Young remains a work in progress – his third-down performance left much to be desired, and he took two sacks – but seeing that progress doesn’t require a squint. Most of the best performances of Young’s career have come between last November and now.

A replay of Daniels’s elbow bending in the wrong direction prompted a relatable exclamation of “oh shit” from Tom Brady, watching from the Fox booth. Daniels throws with his right arm (ie: not the one injured here), but that’s only of mild comfort to the Commanders. Washington head coach Dan Quinn said after the game that Daniels had indeed dislocated his elbow again, although no bones were broken. The quarterback is expected to return at some point this season.

Spare a thought for the players in the Eagles’ win over the Titans in Nashville. Fox reported that the turf (not the air) temperature reached 157F (69.4C) and some players’ cleats even melted . “It was hot as shit, everybody was as hot as shit,” Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said after his team’s 24-20 win. “I didn’t play a snap and I had to get an IV.”

The Browns beat the Buccaneers behind an unusually competent effort from their pitiful quarterback, Deshaun Watson. The QB on the losing end was Baker Mayfield, whom the Browns chased off after 2021 so that they could sign Watson to the worst contract in football history. Watson has spent his Browns career either injured, ineffective, or suspended after the league looked into allegations of serial sexual misconduct. Watson’s 24-of-30 effort for 238 yards and two touchdowns doesn’t absolve him, or the Browns, of anything but does save the franchise a bit of short-term embarrassment that would have come with Mayfield beating them.

The Panthers enjoyed one of the most dominant wins of the young season, a 34-3 destruction of a Falcons team that again started third-string QB Cooper Rush (and also played training camp darling Jack Strand, an undrafted rookie from Division II Minnesota State-Moorhead). The story here was about a QB with a more robust pedigree: Bryce Young, whose career looks like it might amount to something after all. The 2023 No 1 pick came on strong in the last few months of last season and played well. Young averaged eight yards per throw while avoiding interceptions. Even better, Young’s sharpest connection was with 2025 first-round wideout Tetairoa McMillan, who torched Atlanta corner AJ Terrell for a 26-yard completion in the first three minutes and went on to a 101-yard day. Young remains a work in progress – his third-down performance left much to be desired, and he took two sacks – but seeing that progress doesn’t require a squint. Most of the best performances of Young’s career have come between last November and now.

articles.content:
Liverpool look stronger at the back, youngsters shine for Brighton and Brentford, and James Trafford makes his England case with Leeds

In the week that 16-year-old Max Dowman has been thrust into the spotlight , it was another teenager who gave us a glimpse of the future in Brighton’s impressive win over Arsenal. Charalampos Kostoulas – nicknamed ‘Babis’ in his homeland, in homage to former Argentina striker Gabriel Batistuta – has already started twice as many Premier League games as he did in his first season in English football, when he was a backup for Danny Welbeck. The 19-year-old repaid Fabian Hürzeler’s faith in him against the reigning champions. Despite his tender years, Kostoulas already possesses the physical attributes to mix it with the best. He caused Gabriel Magalhães and company problems all afternoon, capping it off with a brilliant goal from 25 yards, his third in eight days. “We always knew that he’s capable of scoring goals out of nowhere,” said Hürzeler. “He just has this intrinsic motivation of really improving every day. He gets more and more professional, he understands the demands from the Premier League more, he understands our demands.” Ed Aarons

Alexander Isak may have been Liverpool’s match-winner on Andoni Iraola’s return to Bournemouth, but it was an afternoon to celebrate defence rather than attack. Liverpool’s front four, signed for a combined £400m, were shorn of fluidity and chemistry. The real stars were in defence, with Ronald Araújo strong at right-back and Jérémy Jacquet commanding at centre-back. Liverpool have kept three straight clean sheets in the league for the first time since the start of 2024-25, and Jacquet’s partnership with Virgil van Dijk is blossoming. Last week the 21-year-old, a £60m arrival from Rennes, was named in Zinedine Zidane’s France squad in his first senior call-up. “He is adapting really well to the Premier League ,” Iraola said of Jacquet. “I think in the first games, physically he was feeling the change of rhythm, he was finishing with cramps, really tired and we had to sub him. Today [Sunday] has been a step forward.” Ben Fisher

Michael Carrick is far too phlegmatic to describe anything in such terms, but Manchester United’s game at Fulham was a must-win for the head coach – and they failed to win it. Going into the extended international break, United desperately needed a positive, but instead had to settle for a draw, clinched by Matheus Cunha. Despite the late equaliser, there were plenty of worrying signs for Carrick. One might have assumed United would come out all guns blazing at Craven Cottage in an attempt to seize control and change the narrative after a poor week, in which they had lost twice. Yet for long periods they were lethargic, lacking intensity off the ball and looking short of snap and fizz in the final third. Of particular concern to Carrick will be United’s profligacy in attack; they managed 29 shots at Fulham, but only six were on target and their goal needed a huge deflection to beat Bernd Leno. Dominic Booth

With Dean Henderson absent from the Crystal Palace net and upcoming England squad, James Trafford had a further chance to impress Thomas Tuchel. Admittedly, Trafford spent a long time being very quiet and barely had anything to do in the first half, but after the break he showed why he is so highly thought of, costing Leeds more than £40m in the summer. The former Manchester City goalkeeper made a fine save down to his right from a Yéremy Pino free-kick when the Spaniard surprised him from the edge of the box. Furthermore, Trafford’s ability with the ball at his feet makes him a true competitor for Jordan Pickford at international level. If he carries on being a calming influence at Elland Road, he could become his country’s No 1 before too long. Will Unwin

For an initial €20m (£17.2m) outlay to Ajax last summer, Brian Brobbey appears a bargain at No 9 as the 24-year-old’s hat-trick in Sunderland’s 5-3 loss at Manchester City underlined. These were the Dutchman’s first goals – all poacher’s finishes – in the sixth game of the season but Régis Le Bris had been unconcerned. “It’s really positive for a striker [to score three] – when you don’t score it’s still possible to tell the story differently [that he is failing] but for us it is really clear that he is a good striker and he’s getting better game after game. It’s just a question of time,” said the manager, who believes his striker is improving. Brobbey was left disappointed despite his hat-trick. “It’s hard being on the losing side when you’re scoring three goals,” he said. Jamie Jackson

All three promoted clubs have victories on the board following Coventry’s gutsy win at Nottingham Forest . By far the best team in last season’s Championship, Coventry’s struggles were in danger of souring their return to the top division. Jay Dasilva’s superb goal and an organised performance offered a remarkable turnaround from last Sunday’s hammering by Brighton. They now enter the bumper international break with optimism. As Frank Lampard noted, facing Arsenal, Manchester City and Brighton in three of their first four games has not been a kind reintroduction. Their defender, Stephen Mfuni, 18, delivered an assured Premier League debut. On loan from Manchester City, Mfuni received rave reviews in a four-month spell at Watford, another youthful defender to make a strong impression, alongside Jannik Schuster at Brentford and Luka Vuskovic at Brighton. Though was it Mfuni that Caleb Yirenkyi tripped over for the VAR decision that denied Forest an equaliser? Zapruder-esque footage from Forest fans suggests it might have been. John Brewin

By the end, the talk had switched to Brentford’s attacking potency, both from set plays and through the quiet probing of Mikkel Damsgaard, but this was a victory rooted in their defending. Jannik Schuster arrived from Salzburg in the summer for a fee of around £16m and is already beginning to look like a typically astute Brentford signing. The 20-year-old made his league debut as a substitute for the injured Nathan Collins against Sunderland, made his first start against Bournemouth and excelled against Chelsea, making 12 clearances, winning three aerial duels and blocking three shots. Perhaps more than anything else in football, defending is about structure but, still, it was striking to compare Schuster’s performance with that of the three Chelsea central defenders, who cost a combined £127m despite Levi Colwill being a youth product. Jonathan Wilson

In attempting to get a handle on the latest Tottenham horror show, Saturday’s 3-2 home defeat by Aston Villa , Roberto De Zerbi bemoaned his side’s lack of resolve in tough moments. “Leaders have to be leaders”, he said. That Spurs lack leaders is clear but the void makes itself felt not just in weak defending. A dominant first half ended goalless for Spurs because of an absence of anyone grabbing the game by the scruff of the neck. The £50m signing Mohammed Kudus came on at half-time, but only made things worse. Only when James Maddison came on and Kudus went wide did Spurs regain shape and focus. De Zerbi appears to be taking a cautious approach to reintegrating Maddison, who missed a year of football with an ACL injury, but the Spurs No 10 has the ability and the self-confidence to impose himself on Premier League matches. De Zerbi might need to hasten his reintroduction. Paul MacInnes

Following an ultimately hard fought 2-1 home win against Hull , Newcastle and their new manager, Matthias Jaissle, were left with a respectable eight points from the opening five Premier League games. But what have we learned along the way? Principal conclusions include: 1) Keeping the outstanding England left back, Lewis Hall this summer was imperative; 2) There will be times when Sean Steur requires resting, and moments when he makes mistakes, but the 18-year-old midfielder is an immensely exciting talent capable of shaping games; 3) A current tally of nine injured first-team players suggests Jaissle needs to modify his training regime; 4) Newcastle’s current lack of an orthodox centre forward and a natural No 10 makes Jaissle’s preferred 4-2-3-1 system hard to pull off; his squad are arguably better suited to playing three at the back; 5) Judging by Newcastle’s refusal to surrender to a spirited Hull, Jaissle is winning hearts and minds. Louise Taylor

Aside from the latest VAR nonsense, Stuart Attwell’s biggest call at Hill Dickinson Stadium was to show Abdul Fatawu a second yellow card for simulation. Despite Gary O’Neil’s claim to the contrary, the referee deserves all credit for doing so. The Ipswich winger was enjoying a productive afternoon and Everton were seething over the decision to disallow Thierno Barry’s header when Fatawu anticipated contact from James Garner and dived. He became only the third player in the last six Premier League seasons to receive a second yellow card for simulation. O’Neil admitted Fatawu had “moved his leg towards it a bit” and that he had spoken to the 22-year-old about not giving the referee a decision to make. But the Ipswich manager’s insistence there was “no desperate need for the referee to get involved” jarred. It was cheating, plain and simple, and the game would benefit from referees punishing it more frequently. It is also a disgrace that Fatawu was racially abused online afterwards. Ipswich and the relevant authorities are investigating the incident. Andy Hunter
