articles.content:
The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay

‘A chtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did feel quite shouty. The only thing was, no one on the Feistritzer Alm – a peaceful sweep of Alpine pasture at the meeting of Austria and Italy – was paying any attention to it at all.

Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.

My husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the old Gasthof Alte Post , we’d bought a loaf from the bäckerei , climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.

We were hiking the Alpe Adria , a long-distance trail jointly developed by Austria, Slovenia and Italy that runs from the foot of Grossglockner (Austria’s highest mountain at 3,798 metres) to the Adriatic coast. At 750km (466 miles), the full trail is too long for most people’s summer holidays. But a 135km (84 mile) loop – moderate-graded, doable in a week, with walking days of 15-24km (9-15 miles) – has been created where the three nations meet, to offer a multicultural taster. It’s an appealing idea; hikers love circuiting multiple countries – just look at the numbers crowding the Tour du Mont Blanc these days. While the Alpe Adria loop isn’t quite as dramatic as that, it does offer a much quieter alternative.

We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispy bitterballen before boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.

Now, on the Feistritzer Alm, a day and a half into the walk, Austria was behind us (for the time being) and Italy beckoned, beautifully. Just around the hill from the Schutzhütte Oisternig sat the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (or the Chiesa Madonna della Neve/Almkapelle Maria Schnee, depending on your linguistic preferences); beyond spread deep-green foothills and the jagged Julian Alps, sawing into a hot-blue sky.

From here, the rest of the day was all downhill, a drop through blessed shade and butterflies, on paths weaving through the pines and peeping out to the peaks, to end in the village of Valbruna, at the Valbruna Inn . We had a wonderful room, and spent time on our balcony, gazing past the geraniums to the sheer Jôf Fuart range, which reaches up to 2,666 metres.

We also spent time in the hotel’s Julius Kugy Library, a cosy den of books on alpinism, named after a writer-mountaineer legend. Born in 1858 to a Slovenian family in Gorizia – then part of the Austrian empire, now in Italy – Kugy is credited with opening up the Julian Alps. He never lost his reverence for nature, always encouraging others to explore with respect, curiosity and awe. I picked up one of his books and read from his introduction: “[This] tries to describe the mountains as a source of happiness, because such they were in my life.”

I couldn’t have agreed more and, with great happiness, we continued the next morning, following the Alpe Adria from Valbruna, across the Saisera River and up through fir and spruce to the Sanctuary of Monte Lussari , a ridge-top pilgrim church and hamlet, where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared in 1360. I was less moved by the miracle, or the shops selling branded tote bags, liqueurs and slippers, than by the mountains scattered far and wide. We lingered to enjoy the view, then descended via alpenrose and ambling goats to Tarvisio, finding a different kind of happiness in the town’s gelaterias. Then, later that evening, we sat with cold beers on our balcony at the Hotel Nevada , watching as a storm crashed through, briefly erasing every mountain.

The next day brought more joy as the trail took us along the woodland-weaving Sentiero del Orso and then via a busy cycle path to the Fusine lakes. These twin glacial bowls are so arrestingly blue-green you’d think they’d been AI-ed if you weren’t standing right there. We found a quiet spot to picnic, listening to the whinnying of little grebes and staring beyond the dazzling water to the afternoon’s challenge via the rocks ahead: the haul up to Rifugio Zacchi .

The Alpe Adria loop usually ends each day in a valley bottom, where there are plenty of inns. But not tonight. Zacchi sits at 1,380 metres, tight-hugged by the intimidating peaks that mark the Slovenian border. After a muggy, magical ascent through forest to the refuge, I sat on the terrace, drinking a superb Aperol spritz, and stared at them, transfixed; a few booms of thunder rippled, just in case the power of nature had been in doubt.

The food at Zacchi was excellent – venison ragù, chargrilled peppers, potato-pancake-like frico , made with local montasio cheese. Also excellent was the fact that, in a stroke of luck, we had a dorm to ourselves. We woke, refreshed and ready for the next border hop.

The most striking route would have been over the forbidding-looking Vratca Pass. The Alpe Adria took us there, for views east into Triglav national park, but didn’t cross. Instead, the trail backtracked down on the Italian side to follow a path through the verdant Sava Valley to the outdoorsy town of Kranjska Gora.

It was a pleasant entrance into Slovenia; however, our exit was spectacular. To get back to Austria the next day, we had to cross the Karavanke Alps and conquer the highest point of our route, the 1,842-metre Schwarzkogel. It was an unrelenting climb, at first amid pasture and shingle roofs, with sublime views to the Julian peaks, then deep in forest serenaded by thrushes, streams trickling to our side.

As we neared the top, we could see south across Slovenia’s surging summits, north across Carinthia’s electric-blue lakes and low hills. Squat white marker-stones began to appear too, strung along the ridge’s spine – an international border marked more casually than most front gardens. We slalomed between the posts, enjoying both the freedom of movement and the majesty of nature. For millennia the Alps have been physical and cultural barriers. The Alpe Adria is a bringing together; a source of mountain happiness.

paragraphs: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay

‘A chtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did feel quite shouty. The only thing was, no one on the Feistritzer Alm – a peaceful sweep of Alpine pasture at the meeting of Austria and Italy – was paying any attention to it at all.

Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.

My husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the old Gasthof Alte Post , we’d bought a loaf from the bäckerei , climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.

We were hiking the Alpe Adria , a long-distance trail jointly developed by Austria, Slovenia and Italy that runs from the foot of Grossglockner (Austria’s highest mountain at 3,798 metres) to the Adriatic coast. At 750km (466 miles), the full trail is too long for most people’s summer holidays. But a 135km (84 mile) loop – moderate-graded, doable in a week, with walking days of 15-24km (9-15 miles) – has been created where the three nations meet, to offer a multicultural taster. It’s an appealing idea; hikers love circuiting multiple countries – just look at the numbers crowding the Tour du Mont Blanc these days. While the Alpe Adria loop isn’t quite as dramatic as that, it does offer a much quieter alternative.

We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispy bitterballen before boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.

Now, on the Feistritzer Alm, a day and a half into the walk, Austria was behind us (for the time being) and Italy beckoned, beautifully. Just around the hill from the Schutzhütte Oisternig sat the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (or the Chiesa Madonna della Neve/Almkapelle Maria Schnee, depending on your linguistic preferences); beyond spread deep-green foothills and the jagged Julian Alps, sawing into a hot-blue sky.

From here, the rest of the day was all downhill, a drop through blessed shade and butterflies, on paths weaving through the pines and peeping out to the peaks, to end in the village of Valbruna, at the Valbruna Inn . We had a wonderful room, and spent time on our balcony, gazing past the geraniums to the sheer Jôf Fuart range, which reaches up to 2,666 metres.

We also spent time in the hotel’s Julius Kugy Library, a cosy den of books on alpinism, named after a writer-mountaineer legend. Born in 1858 to a Slovenian family in Gorizia – then part of the Austrian empire, now in Italy – Kugy is credited with opening up the Julian Alps. He never lost his reverence for nature, always encouraging others to explore with respect, curiosity and awe. I picked up one of his books and read from his introduction: “[This] tries to describe the mountains as a source of happiness, because such they were in my life.”

I couldn’t have agreed more and, with great happiness, we continued the next morning, following the Alpe Adria from Valbruna, across the Saisera River and up through fir and spruce to the Sanctuary of Monte Lussari , a ridge-top pilgrim church and hamlet, where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared in 1360. I was less moved by the miracle, or the shops selling branded tote bags, liqueurs and slippers, than by the mountains scattered far and wide. We lingered to enjoy the view, then descended via alpenrose and ambling goats to Tarvisio, finding a different kind of happiness in the town’s gelaterias. Then, later that evening, we sat with cold beers on our balcony at the Hotel Nevada , watching as a storm crashed through, briefly erasing every mountain.

The next day brought more joy as the trail took us along the woodland-weaving Sentiero del Orso and then via a busy cycle path to the Fusine lakes. These twin glacial bowls are so arrestingly blue-green you’d think they’d been AI-ed if you weren’t standing right there. We found a quiet spot to picnic, listening to the whinnying of little grebes and staring beyond the dazzling water to the afternoon’s challenge via the rocks ahead: the haul up to Rifugio Zacchi .

The Alpe Adria loop usually ends each day in a valley bottom, where there are plenty of inns. But not tonight. Zacchi sits at 1,380 metres, tight-hugged by the intimidating peaks that mark the Slovenian border. After a muggy, magical ascent through forest to the refuge, I sat on the terrace, drinking a superb Aperol spritz, and stared at them, transfixed; a few booms of thunder rippled, just in case the power of nature had been in doubt.

The food at Zacchi was excellent – venison ragù, chargrilled peppers, potato-pancake-like frico , made with local montasio cheese. Also excellent was the fact that, in a stroke of luck, we had a dorm to ourselves. We woke, refreshed and ready for the next border hop.

The most striking route would have been over the forbidding-looking Vratca Pass. The Alpe Adria took us there, for views east into Triglav national park, but didn’t cross. Instead, the trail backtracked down on the Italian side to follow a path through the verdant Sava Valley to the outdoorsy town of Kranjska Gora.

It was a pleasant entrance into Slovenia; however, our exit was spectacular. To get back to Austria the next day, we had to cross the Karavanke Alps and conquer the highest point of our route, the 1,842-metre Schwarzkogel. It was an unrelenting climb, at first amid pasture and shingle roofs, with sublime views to the Julian peaks, then deep in forest serenaded by thrushes, streams trickling to our side.

As we neared the top, we could see south across Slovenia’s surging summits, north across Carinthia’s electric-blue lakes and low hills. Squat white marker-stones began to appear too, strung along the ridge’s spine – an international border marked more casually than most front gardens. We slalomed between the posts, enjoying both the freedom of movement and the majesty of nature. For millennia the Alps have been physical and cultural barriers. The Alpe Adria is a bringing together; a source of mountain happiness.

articles.content:
Arthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every year

W hen Arthur Plummer retired at 65, he bought a secondhand bicycle. His sister was a member of a cycling club for seniors in the Canadian city of Waterloo, Ontario, where they lived, and Plummer joined, too, becoming one of the club’s youngest members. Now he is 92 and its oldest member – but he still cycles thousands of kilometres every year. His odometer for this year so far reads 4,270km (2,650 miles). After our conversation, he intends to cycle another 40km.

“I love cycling,” he says. “Wherever I go, even if I ride on the same roads, there’s something new happening. When I get on my bike, I feel great. I come home at about 3pm and I feel exhausted. However, it’s the nicest feeling. It’s exhilarating, and it’s resulted in me being extremely healthy.”

Even when, in his late 80s, Plummer developed polymyalgia rheumatica (an inflammatory condition that causes pain, stiffness and inflammation in the shoulders, neck and hips) and was unable to walk, cycling helped him to move again. “I was in a wheelchair and I would sit outside in my driveway and people would go by and I felt trapped,” he says. “I can’t walk,” he thought, “but if I can get on my bike, I bet I could ride.” So that’s what he did.

Although his legs are strong, walking is still uncomfortable; he has a shortened stride and sometimes struggles to keep up with his wife and friends on holiday. Cycling , on the other hand, brings freedom. Plummer has cycled “on every street you can go on” within 100 sq miles (260 sq km) of where he lives. He often takes his bike on the bus so that he can explore farther afield. “I’m looking for new vistas,” he says.

Plummer wasn’t into sports when he was growing up. His parents, he says, “were not well off”. His father worked in a rubber factory, his mother looked after the home and worked as a waiter, and as a sales assistant in a clothes shop. “There were few luxuries. It was a tough life, but it was a good life.

“In 1934, when I was born, it was the norm to not have money.” His classmates were either rich or poor. “And we stayed apart. It was an advantage to be poor, because you had more friends.”

There wasn’t time to cycle in younger adulthood. After college, Plummer worked as an estimator or quantity surveyor, initially on hydro projects in northern Quebec, before returning to Ontario. Along the way, he became a single parent to three daughters, then aged nine, 11 and 13 – “a wonderful experience”, he says.

Later, he partnered with four others in a company that oversaw construction and renovation projects in schools. But he found the job very stressful and when a colleague had a heart attack, he decided he needed to change jobs. At 50, he became a municipal building inspector, a job he did until retirement. Sometimes, he would drive past a colleague who commuted by bike, even pedalling through a winter snow squall. “You know how you remember some things for ever in your life? I thought: ‘Wow, he’s an avid cyclist.’”

When he took up cycling himself, Plummer rode at a maximum sustained speed of 25kph. Now that’s dropped to between 15 and 20kph, and he has reduced his distance target to 5,000km a year. He is mindful of risks – he stopped skiing at 90 for fear of breaking a limb – but he has gone over his handlebars six times, and a few years ago he collided with a car that ran a red light. Mercifully, he escaped with cuts and bruises.

“I apparently went head first on to the road, broke my helmet and passed out. People tell me that when I woke, I ran straight to my bike,” he says. “There is a kind of a connection between the rider and the bike.”

A couple of years ago, Plummer moved into a high-rise apartment, “living the urban lifestyle downtown”, and now keeps his carbon-fibre Cannondale bike on a rack next to his bed. “My bike is my best friend,” he says. “We are a team.” If Plummer wakes in the night, he acknowledges his bike “with a greeting: ‘Hey there, buddy’”.

Cycling brings its own momentum. “I am so full of energy, I can’t believe it myself sometimes. I want to get out and use that energy to cycle,” Plummer says. “I hope my last day is on my bike. I have a saying: I’m cycling to eternity and it’s further than I thought.”

articles.title: The agony of life with chronic body odour: ‘I swear I’ve tried every deodorant’
articles.summary: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers If Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window. She likewise tries to avoid people at the cinema or on planes, even if it means paying extra – whatever it takes to avoid being too close to others. She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers

I f Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window. She likewise tries to avoid people at the cinema or on planes, even if it means paying extra – whatever it takes to avoid being too close to others.

She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.”

For more than a decade, 66-year-old Hayat lived with bromhidrosis: chronic body odour. Though the term applies to BO from any cause, including poor hygiene, it is more typically driven by a bacterial imbalance or other health issue.

For those individuals, it’s not a question of bathing more often, or switching to a higher-strength deodorant: their body is working against them, and the impact can be ruinous. “Fifteen minutes after a shower, they’ve already started smelling,” says Chris Callewaert, a senior research fellow at Ghent University, Belgium, and one of the few scientists in the world specialising in body odour.

Callewaert describes bromhidrosis as a natural bodily process gone awry, most typically involving the apocrine glands. These are concentrated around the armpits, breasts and groin, and secrete lipids, steroids and proteins. This sweat itself is odourless; BO is produced by the natural bacteria on the skin and inside the hair follicles as they digest the fatty secretion.

In people with apocrine bromhidrosis – that is to say, abnormal or abnormally offensive body odour – some aspect of that process is out of balance, says Callewaert. They may have overactive apocrine glands, perhaps, or an overabundance of specific “smelly bacteria”.

Body odour can come on abruptly: with puberty, a change to the microbiome, a disease affecting the metabolism, or even as a side-effect of medication. But once established, it can prove difficult to shift, Callewaert says. “It’s often multifactorial, and not easy to perceive the deeper origin or to fix it. Sometimes people have been stuck with this for many, many years.”

In Hayat’s case, she developed bromhidrosis along with hyperhidrosis – excessive and uncontrollable sweating, a distinct but often coexistent condition – during menopause. In 2007, when she was 48, she had an ovary removed, which disrupted her oestrogen production. “After that, life started to change. It was absolutely disruptive,” she says.

She was constantly overheated, “burning inside” even during New York’s freezing winters. On the subway, she would be wearing a sleeveless top and sandals, her hair dripping wet from sweat, while other commuters were in heavy coats, boots and scarves. “People were looking at me like I was crazy,” she says.

That was only half of it. She also smelled – from her armpits, under her breasts, her groin. Her fellow New Yorkers did not hold back from letting her know. Some covered their noses as she passed, or moved away from her. “Those were the polite ones,” Hayat says. Others verbally abused her; more than once, she was harassed off the train. “It was awful, a total nightmare.”

Hayat understood the strong reactions: “It’s normal – you don’t want to be next to anybody who smells bad.” But over-the-counter and prescription remedies made no difference. Hayat estimates that she spent thousands of dollars searching fruitlessly for relief. “At one point I was seeing endocrinologists, gynaecologists, general cardiologists … I had a whole team, trying to find out what was going on in my body.”

There is no set diagnostic threshold at which bad BO becomes bromhidrosis, which makes it difficult to estimate how common it is. A 2024 review described it as prevalent, at least in the west, and taking a “significant” toll on patients’ social and psychological wellbeing. Yet there is very little focused attention on the condition or specialised support.

“There is not a lot of information, and I think that’s sort of indicative. People are ashamed,” Ballard says. “They don’t talk about it with their healthcare providers, even their friends.”

The stigma over BO persists despite it being a natural part of life, from puberty to pregnancy and beyond. According to the IHS, an estimated 50% of the 1.6m women entering menopause annually in the US alone experience increased underarm sweat and odour.

Ballard says a diagnosis of bromhidrosis is tied to “the level of distress it’s causing a person”, and its effect on their wellbeing and day-to-day function: “How much is this impacting your self-esteem, your confidence, your social life?”

There are strategies that can help with alleviating the odour, she says – from the straightforward (using antibacterial soap, avoiding certain fabrics, improving laundry practices) to the unexpected (laser hair removal or waxing, which limit sites for bacteria, and Botox, which reduces sweat production) and, increasingly, hi-tech.

The miraDry, for instance, is an FDA-approved handheld microwave device that destroys the sweat glands, odour glands and hair follicles in the armpits, and has proved to be effective at managing hyperhidrosis, and sometimes bromhidrosis too.

But, often, even a combination of strategies can only do so much to improve the smell. Meanwhile, managing the social anxiety, second-guessing and paranoia is a separate concern. “You feel like people are judging you, that they think it’s your fault, when you’ve perhaps tried everything,” Ballard says. “It can really spiral.”

The toll can be far-reaching. “People will choose jobs where they can work from home, or skip certain social occasions where their odour could be more apparent … You may hesitate to hug someone or get too close to other people.”

Having been diagnosed with hyperhidrosis as a child, Ellie, 30, began struggling with body odour as she got older. She had wanted to pursue teaching, “but I just couldn’t imagine standing in front of a room full of students all sweaty, fearing smelling bad,” she says.

She now works as an accounting assistant. “There were several career paths I wanted to pursue but didn’t.” She considers herself fortunate to not have been so affected in her intimate relationships.

Many people with bromhidrosis report it negatively affecting their confidence and success in dating, but Ellie says her husband, who has known her since she was a teenager, has always been “completely unfazed”. She was, however, very nearly dissuaded from having children, for fear of passing on her conditions.

But Ellie now has a young daughter: “While excessive sweating and body odour is extremely unfortunate, it is not a reason to not want to live. Even if I do end up passing this down, I will be the best advocate possible for my daughter.”

With doctors having been, generally, “pretty dismissive”, Ellie has developed her own coping strategies, such as wearing only cotton socks and never leaving the house without a full change of clothes on hand. “I swear I’ve tried every deodorant on the market.”

Added to the frustrations and challenges of managing her bromhidrosis are other people’s assumptions – that she is either oblivious to how she smells, or wilfully not doing anything about it. “Don’t think we don’t realise. Odds are, we’re trying everything we can to mask it, and get rid of it, but sometimes there is no way.”

Callewaert’s research has found that people who know or fear that they have BO are actually more attentive to personal hygiene than others. But, he says, the anxious striving to get on top of bromhidrosis can worsen the problem by further imbalancing the microbiome and stoking the production of sweat. “They have stress and, as such, they have odour, and because they have odour, they have more stress: it’s self-enforcing.”

Over time, bromhidrosis can become as much a psychological issue as a physiological one. People with the condition often self-isolate, exacerbating the negative effect on wellbeing, and they might develop anxiety or depression, says Callewaert: “On average, their quality of life is lower.”

Faced with “embarrassing situations and mistreatment”, Hayat organised her life around managing others’ discomfort. Aged 50, she learned to drive and got a car so that she might bypass public transport – no mean feat in New York – and began flying business class for the extra space. “Economically, it was a sacrifice, but for my wellbeing, it was perfect to be as far away as I could from people,” Hayat says.

Her family thought she was behaving irrationally and told her she didn’t even smell: “They used to say: ‘It’s all in your head.” But Hayat didn’t feel that she could trust them over the feedback she was getting in public, “because they love me”.

The experience went so far as to test Hayat’s faith: she says she often turned to the Bible in search of solace and answers. “It was really frustrating: ‘Why me? Why do I have to go through this? What did I do?’”

Her world shrank. “Before menopause, I used to go to the theatre, the movies, to clubs to dance, to restaurants … I stopped all of that.” For more than a decade, she did not go anywhere other than work.

The office was difficult enough. Hayat’s colleagues knew she had a medical condition, but were far from sympathetic, she says. A younger co-worker made a show of using a room spray in Hayat’s presence; she overheard another pair of colleagues talking about her, waving their hands in front of their noses.

Hayat says that her working environment became so hostile that she considered suicide. But eventually, she sought help from her employer’s human resources department, which moved swiftly to find her a spot far from those colleagues and gave her the option of taking action against them for bullying. She declined, but “they made me feel really supported”.

Later in her career, Hayat took advantage of advances in remote working, such as telephone meetings and Zoom calls. She also became more adept at managing her sweating and stress, and with it the smell: “I found ways to survive.”

The strict social penalty against having body odour is worsened by the casualness and flippancy with which the topic is often treated. Even doctors can be dismissive, instructing patients to simply apply more deodorant. “People are being brushed off very easily [because] ‘it’s not life-threatening’,” says Callewaert.

That doesn’t just discount the real suffering of living with bromhidrosis: a subtle change in body odour has been associated with diabetes, Parkinson’s disease and cancer, he says. “Knowing that body odour can be a symptom for underlying diseases, it’s a real sign that needs to be picked up.”

In most cases, however, strong BO stems from the microbiome and poor gut health. A stronger and more offensive body odour is linked to diets high in meat and fast food, and low in vegetables. “Leading a healthy lifestyle will help in smelling better,” Callewaert says. High stress is also a factor.

With the microbiome makeup often stubborn to shift, progress can be slow. Even using antiperspirants and deodorant can exacerbate odour, he says, killing beneficial bacteria while encouraging the more stress-resistant, “smelly” kind to bounce back stronger and more numerous.

At best, these “underarm cosmetics” – widespread only since the mid-20th century – are a short-term solution, Callewaert says. He argues that their use has led to worse BO at the population level, together with the trends, at least in the west, for poor nutrition, high stress and unhealthy guts. So Callewaert – who publicly styles himself as “Dr Armpit” – has been developing what he hopes might prove a silver bullet to BO: his own range of patented probiotic deodorants.

In the meantime, Ballard calls for greater understanding of body odour as a natural product of bacteria on our skin, and compassion for people who might be struggling to keep it in check. Instead of leaping to the assumption that someone who smells must be skipping showers, we might consider their experience, she says.

“Maybe they have bromhidrosis, and it took a lot for them to get out the door to go to work and live their lives. Maybe they have another medical condition, and they have to take medication that has changed their body odour. Or maybe they’re going through menopause … You can notice that you smell something, and stop before the judgment.”

For Hayat, recently retired, the bullying she experienced over her bromhidrosis affected her wellbeing as much as the condition itself. After a decade of the menopause wreaking havoc, her symptoms began to ease. “It got better, thank God,” she says fervently. “It’s still not 100% managed – it’s just that I learned to get by.”

She, too, urges compassion – after all, no one is above body odour. “You can be smelling like roses now, but eventually, for whatever reason, your body’s gonna change.”

paragraphs: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers

I f Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window. She likewise tries to avoid people at the cinema or on planes, even if it means paying extra – whatever it takes to avoid being too close to others.
She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.”

For more than a decade, 66-year-old Hayat lived with bromhidrosis: chronic body odour. Though the term applies to BO from any cause, including poor hygiene, it is more typically driven by a bacterial imbalance or other health issue.

For those individuals, it’s not a question of bathing more often, or switching to a higher-strength deodorant: their body is working against them, and the impact can be ruinous. “Fifteen minutes after a shower, they’ve already started smelling,” says Chris Callewaert, a senior research fellow at Ghent University, Belgium, and one of the few scientists in the world specialising in body odour.

Callewaert describes bromhidrosis as a natural bodily process gone awry, most typically involving the apocrine glands. These are concentrated around the armpits, breasts and groin, and secrete lipids, steroids and proteins. This sweat itself is odourless; BO is produced by the natural bacteria on the skin and inside the hair follicles as they digest the fatty secretion.

In people with apocrine bromhidrosis – that is to say, abnormal or abnormally offensive body odour – some aspect of that process is out of balance, says Callewaert. They may have overactive apocrine glands, perhaps, or an overabundance of specific “smelly bacteria”.

Body odour can come on abruptly: with puberty, a change to the microbiome, a disease affecting the metabolism, or even as a side-effect of medication. But once established, it can prove difficult to shift, Callewaert says. “It’s often multifactorial, and not easy to perceive the deeper origin or to fix it. Sometimes people have been stuck with this for many, many years.”

In Hayat’s case, she developed bromhidrosis along with hyperhidrosis – excessive and uncontrollable sweating, a distinct but often coexistent condition – during menopause. In 2007, when she was 48, she had an ovary removed, which disrupted her oestrogen production. “After that, life started to change. It was absolutely disruptive,” she says.

She was constantly overheated, “burning inside” even during New York’s freezing winters. On the subway, she would be wearing a sleeveless top and sandals, her hair dripping wet from sweat, while other commuters were in heavy coats, boots and scarves. “People were looking at me like I was crazy,” she says.

That was only half of it. She also smelled – from her armpits, under her breasts, her groin. Her fellow New Yorkers did not hold back from letting her know. Some covered their noses as she passed, or moved away from her. “Those were the polite ones,” Hayat says. Others verbally abused her; more than once, she was harassed off the train. “It was awful, a total nightmare.”

Hayat understood the strong reactions: “It’s normal – you don’t want to be next to anybody who smells bad.” But over-the-counter and prescription remedies made no difference. Hayat estimates that she spent thousands of dollars searching fruitlessly for relief. “At one point I was seeing endocrinologists, gynaecologists, general cardiologists … I had a whole team, trying to find out what was going on in my body.”

There is no set diagnostic threshold at which bad BO becomes bromhidrosis, which makes it difficult to estimate how common it is. A 2024 review described it as prevalent, at least in the west, and taking a “significant” toll on patients’ social and psychological wellbeing. Yet there is very little focused attention on the condition or specialised support.
“There is not a lot of information, and I think that’s sort of indicative. People are ashamed,” Ballard says. “They don’t talk about it with their healthcare providers, even their friends.”

The stigma over BO persists despite it being a natural part of life, from puberty to pregnancy and beyond. According to the IHS, an estimated 50% of the 1.6m women entering menopause annually in the US alone experience increased underarm sweat and odour.

Ballard says a diagnosis of bromhidrosis is tied to “the level of distress it’s causing a person”, and its effect on their wellbeing and day-to-day function: “How much is this impacting your self-esteem, your confidence, your social life?”

There are strategies that can help with alleviating the odour, she says – from the straightforward (using antibacterial soap, avoiding certain fabrics, improving laundry practices) to the unexpected (laser hair removal or waxing, which limit sites for bacteria, and Botox, which reduces sweat production) and, increasingly, hi-tech.

The miraDry, for instance, is an FDA-approved handheld microwave device that destroys the sweat glands, odour glands and hair follicles in the armpits, and has proved to be effective at managing hyperhidrosis, and sometimes bromhidrosis too.

But, often, even a combination of strategies can only do so much to improve the smell. Meanwhile, managing the social anxiety, second-guessing and paranoia is a separate concern. “You feel like people are judging you, that they think it’s your fault, when you’ve perhaps tried everything,” Ballard says. “It can really spiral.”

The toll can be far-reaching. “People will choose jobs where they can work from home, or skip certain social occasions where their odour could be more apparent … You may hesitate to hug someone or get too close to other people.”

Having been diagnosed with hyperhidrosis as a child, Ellie, 30, began struggling with body odour as she got older. She had wanted to pursue teaching, “but I just couldn’t imagine standing in front of a room full of students all sweaty, fearing smelling bad,” she says.
She now works as an accounting assistant. “There were several career paths I wanted to pursue but didn’t.” She considers herself fortunate to not have been so affected in her intimate relationships.

Many people with bromhidrosis report it negatively affecting their confidence and success in dating, but Ellie says her husband, who has known her since she was a teenager, has always been “completely unfazed”. She was, however, very nearly dissuaded from having children, for fear of passing on her conditions.

But Ellie now has a young daughter: “While excessive sweating and body odour is extremely unfortunate, it is not a reason to not want to live. Even if I do end up passing this down, I will be the best advocate possible for my daughter.”

With doctors having been, generally, “pretty dismissive”, Ellie has developed her own coping strategies, such as wearing only cotton socks and never leaving the house without a full change of clothes on hand. “I swear I’ve tried every deodorant on the market.”

Added to the frustrations and challenges of managing her bromhidrosis are other people’s assumptions – that she is either oblivious to how she smells, or wilfully not doing anything about it. “Don’t think we don’t realise. Odds are, we’re trying everything we can to mask it, and get rid of it, but sometimes there is no way.”

Callewaert’s research has found that people who know or fear that they have BO are actually more attentive to personal hygiene than others. But, he says, the anxious striving to get on top of bromhidrosis can worsen the problem by further imbalancing the microbiome and stoking the production of sweat. “They have stress and, as such, they have odour, and because they have odour, they have more stress: it’s self-enforcing.”

Over time, bromhidrosis can become as much a psychological issue as a physiological one. People with the condition often self-isolate, exacerbating the negative effect on wellbeing, and they might develop anxiety or depression, says Callewaert: “On average, their quality of life is lower.”

Faced with “embarrassing situations and mistreatment”, Hayat organised her life around managing others’ discomfort. Aged 50, she learned to drive and got a car so that she might bypass public transport – no mean feat in New York – and began flying business class for the extra space. “Economically, it was a sacrifice, but for my wellbeing, it was perfect to be as far away as I could from people,” Hayat says.

Her family thought she was behaving irrationally and told her she didn’t even smell: “They used to say: ‘It’s all in your head.” But Hayat didn’t feel that she could trust them over the feedback she was getting in public, “because they love me”.

The experience went so far as to test Hayat’s faith: she says she often turned to the Bible in search of solace and answers. “It was really frustrating: ‘Why me? Why do I have to go through this? What did I do?’”

Her world shrank. “Before menopause, I used to go to the theatre, the movies, to clubs to dance, to restaurants … I stopped all of that.” For more than a decade, she did not go anywhere other than work.

The office was difficult enough. Hayat’s colleagues knew she had a medical condition, but were far from sympathetic, she says. A younger co-worker made a show of using a room spray in Hayat’s presence; she overheard another pair of colleagues talking about her, waving their hands in front of their noses.

Hayat says that her working environment became so hostile that she considered suicide. But eventually, she sought help from her employer’s human resources department, which moved swiftly to find her a spot far from those colleagues and gave her the option of taking action against them for bullying. She declined, but “they made me feel really supported”.

Later in her career, Hayat took advantage of advances in remote working, such as telephone meetings and Zoom calls. She also became more adept at managing her sweating and stress, and with it the smell: “I found ways to survive.”

The strict social penalty against having body odour is worsened by the casualness and flippancy with which the topic is often treated. Even doctors can be dismissive, instructing patients to simply apply more deodorant. “People are being brushed off very easily [because] ‘it’s not life-threatening’,” says Callewaert.

That doesn’t just discount the real suffering of living with bromhidrosis: a subtle change in body odour has been associated with diabetes, Parkinson’s disease and cancer, he says. “Knowing that body odour can be a symptom for underlying diseases, it’s a real sign that needs to be picked up.”

In most cases, however, strong BO stems from the microbiome and poor gut health. A stronger and more offensive body odour is linked to diets high in meat and fast food, and low in vegetables. “Leading a healthy lifestyle will help in smelling better,” Callewaert says. High stress is also a factor.

With the microbiome makeup often stubborn to shift, progress can be slow. Even using antiperspirants and deodorant can exacerbate odour, he says, killing beneficial bacteria while encouraging the more stress-resistant, “smelly” kind to bounce back stronger and more numerous.

At best, these “underarm cosmetics” – widespread only since the mid-20th century – are a short-term solution, Callewaert says. He argues that their use has led to worse BO at the population level, together with the trends, at least in the west, for poor nutrition, high stress and unhealthy guts. So Callewaert – who publicly styles himself as “Dr Armpit” – has been developing what he hopes might prove a silver bullet to BO: his own range of patented probiotic deodorants.

In the meantime, Ballard calls for greater understanding of body odour as a natural product of bacteria on our skin, and compassion for people who might be struggling to keep it in check. Instead of leaping to the assumption that someone who smells must be skipping showers, we might consider their experience, she says.

“Maybe they have bromhidrosis, and it took a lot for them to get out the door to go to work and live their lives. Maybe they have another medical condition, and they have to take medication that has changed their body odour. Or maybe they’re going through menopause … You can notice that you smell something, and stop before the judgment.”

For Hayat, recently retired, the bullying she experienced over her bromhidrosis affected her wellbeing as much as the condition itself. After a decade of the menopause wreaking havoc, her symptoms began to ease. “It got better, thank God,” she says fervently. “It’s still not 100% managed – it’s just that I learned to get by.”
She, too, urges compassion – after all, no one is above body odour. “You can be smelling like roses now, but eventually, for whatever reason, your body’s gonna change.”

articles.content:
Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus

Victoria Starmer has taken part in a London fashion week show, in one of her first public appearances since her husband, Keir Starmer, stepped down as prime minister.

Lady Starmer appeared at Sunday’s Edeline Lee show. The London-based, Canadian British designer’s clothes are a favourite of the Princess of Wales, and have also been worn by celebrities including singer Taylor Swift and actor and screenwriter Phoebe Waller-Bridge.

Lee’s spring/summer 2027 show took place in the unusual setting of a north London school sports hall. Starmer wore a bright turquoise knitted midi dress with a high neckline, pleated detailing and short, sculptural sleeves, paired with white block-heeled shoes, with her hair worn in loose waves.

Rather than preparations for the show taking place backstage in the usual way, in Lee’s unique show, models were fitted and adjusted in full view of the audience, dancers rehearsed beside the catwalk, while a drone followed proceedings from the high ceiling of the gymnasium.

Starmer was photographed having her makeup done beside the catwalk, against a backdrop of a football net, with makeup and hair products spread out over a table in front of her. Ballerinas stretched beside the catwalk and synchronised swimming-inspired dancers performed in bright red costumes as part of the show, in the school in Chalk Farm.

The collection was based on the Greek myth of Sisyphus, in which a man is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down again each time he reaches the top.

“There’s a general feeling right now of relentlessness, a sisyphean cycle,” Lee said. “I was already thinking about the ballet – dance is incredibly transporting, but the work behind it is so intense, the way dancers train for years, the endless repetition, for one ecstatic moment of performance, and then they’re back in the studio.

“I wanted to acknowledge the rigour and hard work behind that moment – much like the skill and artistry required of my team to present beautiful clothes.”

Throughout Keir Starmer’s time in office, Lady Starmer kept a low public profile, but her “political chic” and “modern British” sense of style was often admired. She has favoured contemporary British brands, including ME+EM, Needle & Thread, and Edeline Lee, whose main creative design studio is based in east London.

At London fashion week’s spring/summer shows in 2024, when her husband was prime minister, Lady Starmer took a front-row seat at Edeline Lee’s show, which took place at Millbank Tower, a former campaign HQ of Labour and the Conservatives, where Reform UK’s central office is now based.

She wore a borrowed £615 cream pussy-bow blouse with a navy polka dot print and matching £715 wide-leg trousers.

It came amid a row over free clothes for Lady Starmer, with Keir Starmer facing an investigation at the time over a possible breach of parliamentary rules around gifts.

He had failed to declare that some of his wife’s designer clothes had been bought for her by his biggest personal donor, Lord Alli. The Sunday Times reported that the Labour peer had paid for a personal shopper, clothes and alterations before and after Starmer became prime minister.

articles.content:
This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes

Schmarr n , or schmarren , Anja Dunk writes, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation, pancake , a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and a batter pudding . Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports in her book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings , it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)

Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, including kaiserschmarren (studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.

All the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important. Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipe in The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who sent his recipe to the New York Times in 1980 in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.

My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes from Dunk and the Discover SüdTirol website , which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft and Hinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book , for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.

As Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.

Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargen kirschwasser , all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.

Both Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.

Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).

Traditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).

Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.

A cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). We also like Dunk’s crunchy flaked almonds, but both are entirely optional. As with the nutmeg, chopped hazelnuts, pecans or walnuts would make a fine substitute for those not concerned with authenticity, and even those who are should know that this can be served with any sort of fruit compote, and is particularly good with plums.

Melt the butter in a medium ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat, leave to brown to a pale golden colour, then take off the heat – reheating will continue the browning process. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.

Put the flour and salt in a large bowl. Separate the eggs, then put the whites in a large glass or metal bowl and the yolks in a smaller bowl.

Beat the milk and cream, if using, into the egg yolks, then whisk into the flour to make a smooth batter. Stir in the lemon zest.

Schmarr n , or schmarren , Anja Dunk writes, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation, pancake , a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and a batter pudding . Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports in her book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings , it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)

Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, including kaiserschmarren (studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.

All the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important. Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipe in The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who sent his recipe to the New York Times in 1980 in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.

My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes from Dunk and the Discover SüdTirol website , which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft and Hinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book , for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.

As Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.

Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargen kirschwasser , all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.

Both Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.

Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).

Traditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).

Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.

A cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). articles.title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
articles.summary: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China .

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay .

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”
